meta.name: Red Hat Certified Engineer (RHCE EX294)
meta.notes: [initial seed: 12 EX294 Ansible-on-RHEL9 scenario questions] | v1.1 (2026-07-03): +10 scenario questions — group_names conditionals, notify/handlers, Ansible Vault, extra-vars precedence, firewalld idempotence, Jinja2 templating over groups, block/rescue/always, check mode caveats, role defaults precedence, loop syntax. Rebalanced correct positions (was 42% top slot).

questions.question: An engineer creates the file `/etc/ansible/hosts` on the control node, but `ansible-inventory --list` for the project still returns an empty inventory when run from `~/ex294/`. The project's `ansible.cfg` in that directory contains a `[defaults]` block with `inventory = ./inventory`. Why does Ansible ignore `/etc/ansible/hosts`?
options: Ansible only reads `/etc/ansible/hosts` when invoked as root; the engineer must use `sudo ansible-inventory`
The project-level `ansible.cfg` overrides the system default — Ansible reads `./inventory`, not `/etc/ansible/hosts`
`/etc/ansible/hosts` must be in YAML for Ansible 2.9+; the INI format has been removed
Inventories under `/etc/` are only honored when `ANSIBLE_CONFIG` is unset, which is never the case after package install
questions.explanation: Ansible's configuration precedence is: ANSIBLE_CONFIG env var → ./ansible.cfg in CWD → ~/.ansible.cfg → /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg. The first match wins for the whole file (no merging). Because the project's `ansible.cfg` sets `inventory = ./inventory`, the system default `/etc/ansible/hosts` is never consulted. INI is still supported (option A's claim about removal is false), and root vs user has no bearing on which config is read.

questions.question: A playbook must run on hosts in the `webservers` group, connecting as user `devops` and escalating to root via sudo without a password prompt. Which combination of play-level keywords is correct?
options: `hosts: webservers`, `remote_user: devops`, `become: true`, `become_method: sudo`
`hosts: webservers`, `user: root`, `become: false` — sudo is implicit when targeting root
`hosts: webservers`, `connection: sudo`, `become_user: devops`
`hosts: webservers`, `remote_user: devops`, `privilege: escalate` — `privilege` is the modern replacement for `become`
questions.explanation: `remote_user` controls who SSHs into the target; `become: true` switches identity after the connection; `become_method: sudo` (the default in most configs) chooses the escalation tool; the default `become_user` is `root`. Passwordless sudo for `devops` must be configured on the target (a sudoers drop-in). `connection:` selects a connection plugin like `ssh`/`local`/`winrm`, not an escalation method, and `privilege` is not a real keyword.

questions.question: A task installs the `httpd` package and is followed by a handler that restarts `httpd`. The engineer wants the handler to run only when the package was actually installed or upgraded — not on every play run. Which task definition achieves this idiomatically?
options: Use `ansible.builtin.dnf` with `state: latest` and `register: pkg_result`, then call the handler from a `when: pkg_result.rc == 0` block
Add `changed_when: true` to force the handler to fire each run, then let the handler decide whether to restart
Use `ansible.builtin.dnf` with `state: present` plus `notify: Restart httpd` — handlers fire only when the task reports `changed`
Place the handler in `pre_tasks` so it always runs before `httpd` is touched
questions.explanation: Handlers in Ansible are notified by tasks and run once at the end of the play, but only if the notifying task reported `changed: true`. The `dnf` module returns `changed` when it installs/upgrades a package and `ok` (unchanged) when the package is already at the requested state. So `state: present` + `notify:` gives "restart only when the install actually changed something" for free — no `when:` plumbing needed. Forcing `changed_when: true` defeats idempotence, and pre_tasks run before normal tasks regardless of changes.

questions.question: An engineer needs to encrypt the file `group_vars/db/vault.yml` so it can be committed to git, while leaving the other group_vars files in plaintext. Which command produces a single-file vault?
options: `ansible-vault encrypt group_vars/db/vault.yml`
`ansible-playbook --encrypt group_vars/db/vault.yml`
`gpg --symmetric group_vars/db/vault.yml` — Ansible Vault delegates to GPG under the hood
`ansible-vault create group_vars/db/vault.yml` — `create` re-encrypts existing files in place
questions.explanation: `ansible-vault encrypt <file>` encrypts an existing plaintext file in place using AES-256 with a password (or vault-id). `ansible-vault create` is for making a brand-new encrypted file — running it against an existing file would overwrite it. `decrypt`, `edit`, `view`, and `rekey` cover the rest of the lifecycle. Ansible Vault is a self-contained format and does not call GPG.

questions.question: A play needs to create the same user account on every host in a group, but the user's primary group differs per host. The engineer sets `group_vars/webservers.yml` with `primary_group: web` and `host_vars/db01.yml` with `primary_group: dba`. On `db01`, which value of `primary_group` does Ansible use?
options: `web`, because group_vars are applied after host_vars
Ansible raises a duplicate-variable error and refuses to run
Whichever file was modified most recently on disk
`dba`, because host_vars override group_vars at the same precedence tier
questions.explanation: Ansible's documented variable precedence (low → high) places `group_vars/all` below `group_vars/<group>` below `host_vars/<host>`. `db01.yml` is host-scoped, so its `primary_group: dba` wins on that host; on other webservers (which have no host_vars) the group value `web` applies. The order is deterministic — Ansible never errors on "duplicate" variables across precedence tiers, and file mtime is irrelevant.

questions.question: A task must create the directories `/srv/app/{cache,logs,uploads}` with mode `0755` on every host. Which task is the most idiomatic Ansible way to do this?
options: Three separate `ansible.builtin.file` tasks, one per directory — loops are discouraged for filesystem operations
A single `ansible.builtin.command` task running `mkdir -p /srv/app/{cache,logs,uploads} && chmod 0755 ...`
A single `ansible.builtin.file` task with `state: directory`, `mode: '0755'`, and `loop: [cache, logs, uploads]` using `path: "/srv/app/{{ item }}"`
An `ansible.builtin.shell` task with brace expansion — only `shell` (not `command`) expands `{a,b,c}`
questions.explanation: The `file` module with `state: directory` is the idempotent, declarative choice; iterating with `loop:` keeps the play DRY and lets Ansible report changed/ok per item. Falling back to `command`/`shell` for filesystem state defeats idempotence checks and the module's permission/owner handling. Three duplicated tasks technically work but waste lines and obscure intent — there's no "loops discouraged" rule.

questions.question: An engineer writes a Jinja2 template `httpd.conf.j2` that should render the server's primary IPv4 address. Which expression is correct?
options: `{{ ansible_default_ipv4.address }}` — pulled from gathered facts
`{{ ansible_facts.ip }}` — top-level shortcut added in Ansible 2.10
`{% ip = lookup('hostname', '-I') %}` — `lookup` runs on the target and returns the first interface
`{{ inventory_hostname }}` — Ansible resolves the inventory name to an IP at template time
questions.explanation: When fact gathering is enabled (the default), Ansible exposes networking facts under `ansible_facts['default_ipv4']` (and the legacy `ansible_default_ipv4` alias). The `.address` key holds the IPv4 address of the interface used to reach the default gateway — exactly what a server config usually wants. `ansible_facts.ip` doesn't exist, `lookup` plugins run on the *controller* (not the target), and `inventory_hostname` is the inventory string verbatim, never resolved to an IP.

questions.question: A role called `webapp` lives in `~/ex294/roles/webapp/`. The engineer wants to call it from `site.yml` so its `tasks/main.yml`, `handlers/main.yml`, and `defaults/main.yml` all load in the standard order. Which play body is correct?
options: Add a top-level `tasks:` block with `- import_tasks: roles/webapp/tasks/main.yml` — roles are just a directory convention
Use the play-level `roles:` keyword (alongside `hosts:`) with `- webapp` as the only entry
Add `- role: webapp` inside `pre_tasks:` — `role:` is only valid in `pre_tasks`
List `roles/webapp` under `vars_files:` — Ansible auto-discovers tasks and handlers from `vars_files` entries
questions.explanation: The canonical way to apply a role is the play-level `roles:` keyword, which Ansible resolves under `roles_path` (project-local `./roles/`, then `~/.ansible/roles`, then `/usr/share/ansible/roles`, etc.). Ansible automatically wires `tasks/`, `handlers/`, `defaults/`, `vars/`, `meta/`, and `templates/` from the role's standard skeleton. `import_role:`/`include_role:` are valid alternatives inside `tasks:`, but pointing `import_tasks:` at a single tasks file skips all the other directories. `vars_files:` only loads variable files.

questions.question: A task uses the `ansible.posix.firewalld` module to open TCP port 8080. The engineer wants the rule to apply immediately *and* survive a reboot. Which parameter combination is required?
options: `state: enabled`, `port: 8080/tcp`, `immediate: true`, `permanent: true`
`state: enabled`, `port: 8080/tcp` — `firewalld` is permanent by default
`state: present`, `port: 8080/tcp`, `runtime: true` — `runtime` is the modern replacement for `immediate`
`state: enabled`, `port: 8080/tcp`, `permanent: true` — the runtime config reloads automatically on the next task
questions.explanation: `firewalld` distinguishes between the *runtime* configuration (active until the daemon restarts) and the *permanent* configuration (written to `/etc/firewalld/`, applied on reload). The Ansible module mirrors this with `immediate: true` (apply now) and `permanent: true` (write to disk). You need both to satisfy "apply now and survive a reboot." `state:` for ports is `enabled`/`disabled`, not `present`/`absent`, and there is no `runtime:` parameter.

questions.question: An engineer needs to attempt a risky migration step, run a cleanup task whether it succeeds or fails, and substitute a fallback configuration only if the migration raised an error. Which Ansible construct expresses this cleanly?
options: Three sequential tasks with `ignore_errors: true` on the first and `when:` guards on the others, inspecting the registered result
A single task with `failed_when: false` and a `notify:` to a handler that decides what to do
A `block:` / `rescue:` / `always:` structure — main steps in `block`, fallback in `rescue`, cleanup in `always`
`pre_tasks:` for the migration, `post_tasks:` for cleanup, and `rescue_tasks:` for the fallback
questions.explanation: Ansible's `block:` / `rescue:` / `always:` mirrors try/except/finally: tasks under `block:` run normally, `rescue:` runs only if a `block:` task failed, and `always:` runs after either path — making it the idiomatic way to express "try X, fall back to Y on error, clean up either way." Hand-rolling the same logic with `ignore_errors` + `register` + `when:` works but is verbose and easy to get wrong. `failed_when: false` only suppresses failure on one task and doesn't branch. `rescue_tasks:` is not a real keyword.

questions.question: An engineer wants the `webapp` role's variables in `defaults/main.yml` to be overridable from `group_vars/webservers.yml`, but its variables in `vars/main.yml` to take precedence over everything except command-line `-e`. Which statement matches Ansible's documented precedence?
options: `defaults/main.yml` sits near the bottom of the precedence chain (overridable by inventory and group_vars), while `vars/main.yml` sits near the top (only `-e` and a few task-level keywords beat it)
`defaults/main.yml` and `vars/main.yml` are equivalent — they're merged at role load time
`defaults/main.yml` always wins because Ansible loads it last
Both are overridden by host facts, regardless of role-internal scope
questions.explanation: Role `defaults/main.yml` is at the very bottom of variable precedence — it exists precisely so callers (inventory, group_vars, host_vars, play vars) can override role defaults without editing the role. Role `vars/main.yml` is near the top — only `-e` (extra vars), task `vars:`, `include_vars`, `set_fact`, and a few task-level keywords beat it. This split is the recommended pattern: defaults are configurable knobs, `vars/` are role-internal constants. Host facts have their own (mid-range) tier and do not override either uniformly.

questions.question: An engineer runs `ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check` and gets `ok`, then runs `--check` and gets `ok` again, but the actual run fails because a templated path doesn't exist on disk. Why didn't `--check` catch it?
options: `--check` only validates YAML, just like `--syntax-check`; the two are aliases
Check mode skips fact gathering, so templated paths that depend on facts are never evaluated

Check mode reports what *would* change without making changes — modules that don't support check mode are skipped, and operations like `file: state: directory` against a parent path that doesn't exist won't be created during the dry run, so dependent checks may falsely pass
`--check` requires `--diff` to actually exercise templates; without it, templates are not rendered
questions.explanation: `--syntax-check` is a parse-only pass (YAML + Ansible keywords). `--check` is dry-run/check mode: Ansible reports the changes each module *would* make, without applying them. Crucially, modules that don't implement check mode are skipped, and any task whose success depends on side effects of a *previous* task (e.g., a directory created earlier in the play) will not see those side effects in check mode — so a later task that templates a file into that not-yet-created directory may pass the dry run but fail for real. Fact gathering still runs in check mode (B is wrong), and templates render normally without `--diff` (D is wrong).

questions.question: A play must run a task only on hosts in the `webservers` group and skip others, without editing the inventory. Which construct fits BEST inside a single playbook targeting all hosts?
options: Put the task in a separate playbook and run it manually on webservers.
Hard-code the webserver IPs in the task.
Delete non-webserver hosts from memory with a shell command.
Use a `when: "'webservers' in group_names"` conditional on the task.
questions.explanation: `group_names` is a magic variable listing the groups the current host belongs to, so `when: "'webservers' in group_names"` runs the task only on hosts in that group while the play still targets all. A separate manual playbook defeats automation, deleting hosts at runtime is not how inventory works, and hard-coding IPs breaks idempotence and reuse.

questions.question: A task installs a package and should only restart the service when the package actually changed. Which Ansible mechanism implements this correctly?
options: Always run a restart task at the end of every play.
Notify a handler from the package task; the handler runs once at the end only if the task reported changed.
Use a shell command to grep the package version and restart conditionally.
Set the restart task to `ignore_errors: true`.
questions.explanation: Handlers are triggered by `notify` and run (once, at the end of the play) only when the notifying task reports a changed state — exactly 'restart only if the package changed'. Always restarting is not idempotent, a shell/grep approach is fragile and non-idempotent, and `ignore_errors` merely suppresses failures rather than gating on change.

questions.question: Sensitive variables (passwords) must live in the repo but never in plaintext. Which Ansible feature encrypts them, and how are they used at runtime?
options: Base64-encode the variables in the playbook.
Put them in the shell environment and echo them into tasks.
Store them in group_vars/all in plaintext but restrict file permissions.
Use Ansible Vault to encrypt the file, and supply the vault password (or a vault-id) at run time so tasks decrypt in memory.
questions.explanation: Ansible Vault encrypts variable files (or single values) at rest in the repo; at run time you provide the vault password or a vault-id (`--ask-vault-pass`/`--vault-id`) and Ansible decrypts the content in memory for the play. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; plaintext group_vars with file permissions is still plaintext; and echoing env vars leaks secrets into process/history.

questions.question: Two variable definitions for the same name exist: one in `group_vars` and one passed with `-e` (extra-vars) on the command line. Which value wins?
options: The group_vars value, because inventory is authoritative.
The extra-vars (`-e`) value, because command-line extra-vars have the highest precedence.
Whichever is alphabetically first.
They are merged into a list automatically.
questions.explanation: In Ansible variable precedence, extra-vars supplied with `-e` on the command line have the highest priority and override group_vars and nearly everything else. Inventory group_vars sit much lower in the precedence order, precedence is not alphabetical, and scalar variables are overridden (not merged into a list) by higher-precedence sources.

questions.question: A playbook must open the `https` service in firewalld and make the change persist across reboots, idempotently. Which task is correct?
options: Use the `command` module to run `firewall-cmd --add-service=https` each run.
Use the `shell` module to append an iptables rule.
Edit /etc/sysconfig manually with the `copy` module.
Use the `ansible.posix.firewalld` module with service=https, state=enabled, permanent=true, and immediate=true.
questions.explanation: The `firewalld` module manages rules idempotently; setting service=https, state=enabled, permanent=true (survives reboot) and immediate=true (applies now) is the correct, idempotent way. A raw `firewall-cmd` command is not idempotent and would report changed every run, editing sysconfig by hand is fragile, and appending iptables rules bypasses firewalld and is not idempotent.

questions.question: A template must render a config file listing every host in the play's group. Which combination generates it?
options: A static `copy` of a pre-written file with the hosts hard-coded.
A Jinja2 `template` task iterating over `groups['webservers']` (using hostvars/facts) to render entries dynamically.
A `lineinfile` task run once per host manually.
A `debug` task printing the hosts to stdout.
questions.explanation: The `template` module renders a Jinja2 template on the controller and copies the result; looping in Jinja2 over `groups['webservers']` (and referencing hostvars) produces a config listing every group member dynamically. A static copy hard-codes hosts, lineinfile edits single lines rather than generating a full list, and debug only prints — it writes no file.

questions.question: A block of tasks may fail, and the playbook must run cleanup tasks whether or not the block succeeds, plus specific recovery only on failure. Which structure fits?
options: Wrap each task in `ignore_errors: true`.
Put all tasks in a single shell script with `set -e`.
Use a `block:` with a `rescue:` section (runs on failure) and an `always:` section (runs regardless).
Use a handler notified at the end.
questions.explanation: Ansible's block/rescue/always mirrors try/except/finally: `block` holds the main tasks, `rescue` runs only if a block task fails (recovery), and `always` runs regardless (cleanup). `ignore_errors` hides failures without structured recovery, a shell script abandons Ansible's task model, and handlers run on change notification, not as failure-handling/cleanup control flow.

questions.question: An engineer wants to preview what a playbook would change without applying it. Which invocation is correct, and what is a key caveat?
options: Run with `--syntax-check`, which shows all changes that would be made.
Use `-vvvv` verbosity, which prevents any change from being applied.
Run normally and then manually revert everything.
Run with `--check` (check mode); it reports would-be changes, but tasks that depend on prior task results may be inaccurate because earlier changes were not actually applied.
questions.explanation: `--check` (check/dry-run mode) reports what would change without applying it; the caveat is that when later tasks depend on the effects of earlier tasks (which did not really run), check-mode output for those tasks can be inaccurate. `--syntax-check` only validates YAML/syntax, running-then-reverting is not a dry run, and `-vvvv` only increases logging — it still applies changes.

questions.question: A reusable role must ship sensible default variable values that a playbook can easily override. Where should those defaults live, and what is their precedence?
options: In `roles/x/defaults/main.yml`, which has the lowest precedence so playbook/inventory vars easily override it.
In `roles/x/vars/main.yml`, which cannot be overridden by the playbook.
In the inventory file, which has the highest precedence.
Hard-coded inside each task, so they cannot change.
questions.explanation: Role defaults belong in `defaults/main.yml`, which sits at the lowest variable precedence precisely so consumers can override them from the playbook, inventory, or extra-vars. `vars/main.yml` has much higher precedence and is hard to override, inventory is not the place for role defaults, and hard-coding values in tasks removes configurability.

questions.question: A task must loop over a list of users and create each one. Which is the current, recommended looping syntax in Ansible?
options: `with_items:` is the only supported syntax and must always be used.
Use `loop:` with the list (e.g., loop: "{{ users }}") and reference each element with `item`.
Copy the task once per user manually.
Use a Jinja2 `for` loop directly around the YAML task.
questions.explanation: Modern Ansible recommends `loop:` for iterating a list, referencing the current element as `item` (e.g., in the user module's name). `with_items` still works but `loop` is the current guidance, copying the task per user is not maintainable, and Jinja2 `for` loops cannot wrap a YAML task block to iterate it — looping is a task-level keyword.
